fetch_http_health.notes: No mixed-content block, no Private Network Access (PNA) preflight block observed in this Chromium build.

implication: In this Chromium-based environment (Electron-embedded Chrome 148, no PNA enforcement observed), an https:// origin page can both fetch() and open a WebSocket to a plain ws://127.0.0.1 (or ws://localhost) local companion server with zero blocking — no mixed-content error, no Private Network Access preflight/permission prompt, no CORS failure (server sends permissive ACAO for the health check; WebSocket handshake itself is not subject to CORS). This particular browser build is therefore not a blocker for a ws://127.0.0.1 companion transport design. Caveat: standard desktop Chrome/Chromium (not this Electron-embedded build) has been rolling out Private Network Access, which as of recent versions can require a permission prompt or block private-network fetches from public https origins depending on version/flags; this probe environment appears to not enforce that gate, so results here may be more permissive than a end user's actual Chrome. Safari and Firefox were not tested in this probe and are known to have stricter or different local-network access behavior (Safari has no PNA gate today but local network access permission prompts exist on iOS/macOS Safari in some contexts). Recommendation: re-run this exact probe in a real end-user Chrome (stable channel, default flags) and in Safari before finalizing on ws://127.0.0.1 as the sole transport; a fallback (e.g. a small native helper registering a custom URL scheme, or a browser extension) should still be considered for browsers/versions that do enforce PNA blocking.
